name: The Duncan Cedar

location.address: Off US Route 101, about 15 miles south of Forks, Washington, near the Olympic National Park boundary
location.neighbourhood: Reached via about 4 miles of unpaved logging road from Highway 101; a boardwalk trail leads from a small roadside pull-off marked only by a tree-shaped sign

access: Discover Pass required ($10 day / $45 annual) as it stands on Washington State DNR land, not inside the national park itself. Reached via a short boardwalk from a small, poorly marked roadside pull-off after about 4 miles of unpaved logging road.
transport: No public transit; about 15 miles south of Forks, WA, off US-101. Roadside/trailhead parking, unpaved final approach.
verify_notes: IMPORTANT HONESTY FLAG for the writer: this tree stands on Washington State Department of Natural Resources land (state school trust land), NOT inside Olympic National Park itself, though it sits close to the park boundary near Kalaloch/Forks and is commonly grouped with the park in visitor writing and in this project's own Wikidata sweep. If delivered, the page must say plainly it is outside the park proper, the way this project already handles day-trip additions elsewhere (real place name, true access, true manager). Currently the largest known western redcedar in the world by volume, and the largest tree of any species in Washington state; discovered by loggers in 1975 and preserved after local advocacy. Status: alive but in a striking condition -- described by Wikipedia as mostly dead wood with just a strip of living bark/cambium keeping one trunk alive, which redcedar's rot resistance lets it sustain for a very long time (a forestry expert quoted saying it may live for centuries more barring external damage); a visitor review independently corroborates it as 'plenty alive' with visible green growth. This mirrors the honest framing already used for the Kalaloch Redcedar (oly_001), a half-collapsed but living tree, so the two could make a strong pair for a story about redcedar survival strategies. Height/diameter/age figures are Wikipedia's own, consistent across secondary sources; girth converted from the 19.4ft/5.9m diameter figure via pi (1853cm). Flag for the writer: this comes out close to oly_001's own recorded girth (1859cm), which may be coincidental rounding in both trees' published 'about six metres through' figures rather than a real match; worth a sanity check against primary measurement sources before publishing both.

name: The Tree of Life
age_estimate: not documented; known as a landmark since at least the 1950s

location.address: Kalaloch Beach, near Kalaloch Campground, Olympic National Park, Washington
location.neighbourhood: On the beach about 200-400 feet from the Kalaloch Campground day-use parking lot; the tree grows over a small eroded creek gap, its roots forming an arch/cave with the trunk suspended above

access: Free, within Olympic National Park; a short, flat walk (a few minutes) from the Kalaloch Campground day-use parking lot onto the beach.
transport: No public transit; on US-101, 34 miles south of Forks, WA. Parking at Kalaloch Campground.
verify_notes: A Sitka spruce whose roots have been undercut by an eroding creek and bluff, leaving the trunk suspended over open air on an arch of exposed roots (locally called a 'root cave'); it is one of the most photographed single trees on the Washington coast. Kalaloch Lodge's own staff, quoted by a secondary source, say it has been a known attraction since at least the 1950s and is 'probably much older than that'; no documented age or measurement was found this pass, so left empty per the honest-gap rule rather than guessed (Sitka spruce as a species can live to about 800 years, which is context, not a claim about this specimen). ALIVE BUT PRECARIOUS, and this must be stated on the page: a Seattle Met feature from July 2025 and multiple 2026-dated travel articles describe continuing erosion beneath it, branches showing decline, and warn 'no one knows how much longer the tree will continue to stand'; as of the most recent 2026 update found this pass it is still standing. This is exactly the kind of honest, time-sensitive caveat this project's tone already uses for other precarious trees (compare the Kalaloch Redcedar, oly_001, similarly framed around damage and decline). Location precision: approximate; no GPS found for the tree itself, only walking directions from the campground (turn right on the beach, walk 200-400 feet), so the pin given is the campground, not the trunk.

name: The Quinault Big Spruce

location.address: South Shore Road, near Rain Forest Resort Village, Lake Quinault, Olympic National Park, Washington
location.neighbourhood: A short, flat 0.4-mile out-and-back trail (the 'Big Spruce Trailhead', a named OSM trail node) starting from the Rain Forest Resort Village parking area on South Shore Road

access: Free; NPS's own page for this trail confirms it is located within Olympic National Park, though the immediate trailhead and lawn area are managed day-to-day by the adjacent Rain Forest Resort Village rather than directly by park staff.
transport: No public transit; on South Shore Road at Lake Quinault. Parking at the Rain Forest Resort Village.
verify_notes: The world's record Sitka spruce (American Forests champion-tree recognition, 922 AFA points per secondary sources) and, by volume, one of the largest trees of any species in the continental US outside the California redwoods/sequoias. NPS's own place page for this trail explicitly locates it inside Olympic National Park, which distinguishes it from the Duncan Cedar (oly_002, on separate WA DNR land outside the park). Reported figures (cross-checked against monumentaltrees.com as a verification-only source, per project rules): roughly 58ft 11in circumference (1796cm), about 18ft 9in diameter, around 191ft tall (58m), crown spread 96ft. Age commonly cited as roughly 1,000 years in visitor sources; treated here as a broad, loosely-derived estimate rather than a documented figure, since no primary dendrological study was found this pass. Access: a short (0.4 mile), flat, out-and-back trail from the resort's parking area; OSM independently maps a 'Big Spruce Trailhead' node at the coordinate used here. Alive: recent (2026-dated) visitor reviews describe it as actively accessible and visited, with no reports of damage or decline found, unlike the other three Olympic entries in this pass which all carry some decline/precarity flag.
